newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Pope sends message to Colombian hostages.
newsitem.headline: Pope sends message to Colombian hostages.

text.p: Pope John Paul sent a message of encouragement on Tuesday to 60 Colombian soldiers held hostage by leftist rebels since last August, saying their ordeal spurred new calls for an end to Colombia's guerrilla war.
"Through your sacrifice you have served the cause of peace and definitely the cause of Colombia's progress," the pope said in an open letter to the captive soliders.
The letter was read to a local radio reporter at Bogota's international airport by Vatican envoy Monsignor Paolo Romeo on his return from Rome.

"The calls being made, the effort being made to open the road to understanding and national reconciliation show that the suffering of those of you who have been deprived of your freedom for many months, and who even had to spend Christmas far from your families, is not in vain," the letter said.
"This has served to create awareness of the need to overcome obstacles to national understanding," it said.
The 60 soldiers were seized by Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas when they overran an army base in a remote, jungle-covered area of southwest Colombia on Aug. 30, 1996.

Fledgling efforts to negotiate their release collapsed in December, thanks largely to mutual antagonisms and deep distrust between the military and the FARC. Adding insult to injury, the rebel group took 10 other soldiers hostage in January in northwestern Choco province.

President Ernesto Samper said last week that there was reason to believe the soliders' release could be arranged in the near future. But he has declined to elaborate on possible negotiations with the FARC, which flatly ruled out the possibility of peace talks after they were proposed by newly appointed Defence Miister Gilberto Echeverry last month.
The FARC, which grew out of peasant militias formed in 1948, is the oldest and largest rebel group in Latin America. It was officially formed as a Marxist, pro-Soviet group in 1964.
